messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Violence: Violence, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Tane, of Samoan descent, was seventy-four when he finally booked an appointment, but the weight of what had happened had settled into his shoulders long before. The physical abuse had occurred during his marriage, not as a single collapsing roof but as a series of sharp, sudden strikes. When he closed his eyes now, he did not see a flowing reel of time. He saw a handful of frozen frames: a hand rising against the lamplight, the kitchen chair skidding across hardwood, the sudden silence before a shout. Each moment sat in his mind like a photograph. Sometimes, when those images surfaced, he was certain the man in the pictures was not entirely himself; the memory felt detached, as if it belonged to a stranger who had merely borrowed his face. When the frames caught him, a fierce heat would bank in his chest and throat. He recognized it as rage on recall, sharp and unbidden. His wife’s corrections came with raised voices and sharp, sweeping gestures. When he was criticised now, even gently, his shoulders would lift in preparation. He was certain that the criticising voice held the same weight as the hand that had once pressed him against the wall. Violence itself—any sharp knock, any sudden movement—caught him off guard. He still avoided the corner grocery store where he had seen the offender years later; seeing her walking toward him, even from a distance, made his breath catch in a familiar way. The offender cues were not merely reminders but invitations to the old fear. Tane had come to believe that the event happened because of the sort of person he was: quiet, uncomplaining, the kind of man who swallowed his own edge. He felt as though he had been handled, not held; an object moved along a counter rather than a person meeting another person. This dehumanization sat heavily beside his conviction that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. His heart could beat fast, but he feared the deeper well had dried up. To keep the water from rising, he had built a life of careful avoidance. He avoided anything that reminded him of the person who harmed him—the specific scent of her perfume, the heavy oak sideboard that had cracked when it fell, even the particular cadence of a man’s laugh that sounded too much like her. When emotions did threaten to surface, he did not let them; he practiced avoiding feelings, allowing himself to feel any strong emotion only if he could immediately anchor it to something else. He distracted himself with the precise work of editing, running a finger down columns of manuscript text, correcting commas, tracing syntax until his mind settled into the familiar architecture of the page. His work as an editor was the arena where his habits took shape. Each morning he sat at his long drafting table, surrounded by drafts and marked-up proofs. When a junior associate leaned over his shoulder and suggested a rewording, Tane’s jaw would tighten. He would nod, but his eyes would drop to the paper, distracting himself from the voice by hunting for typos. Over the weeks and months, this careful retreat had cost him. He stopped attending the staff lunches, avoiding the laughter and the casual critiques that now felt too close to home. His apartment, once filled with shared books and lingering conversations, had become a quiet vault. He kept the curtains drawn in the evenings, not from the dark, but from the particular way the streetlights cast long, familiar shadows across the rug. The habit had grown thick enough to notice. One Tuesday, while correcting a stubborn paragraph, Tane found himself staring at the inked corrections, his chest tight with a rage that had nowhere to go. He realized he was bracing for a strike that would not come, afraid that if he let go even slightly, the emotions would flood back and sweep him away. When the intake specialist had read his checklist, the PCL5 total had settled at 77, a number that matched the quiet heaviness of his days. He sought help not because the abuse was fresh, but because the isolation had become too heavy to carry alone. What he hoped for was simple: to read the manuscript of his own life without constantly searching for the editor’s red pen, to trust that he was still a person, not just a thing being handled.
